Introduction

Auralization is a word I heard several times a day from my very first day as a PhD student. Since auralization means recreating sound fields in virtual environments, it has been bound up with virtual reality (VR) from birth. When I started my PhD in 2013, hardly anyone knew what VR was. Two years later VR was all the rage, hyped until every man, woman and child had heard of it. Two years after that, the investment frenzy was over, VR was yesterday’s news, and everything went quiet again. Yet for all the hype in industry, academia seems to have been largely unaffected. In recent years more and more groups have taken up auralization and acoustic virtual reality (AVR), and the chances of winning EU funding in this area are fairly good. The groups vary widely in quality and produce results of every kind, but the field as a whole is on the rise. What it needs now is to find its industrial applications quickly, a place where it can really prove its worth, so that such a fascinating field can keep growing.

Note: most of the videos in this article have binaural soundtracks, so put on headphones to hear the 3D effect.

1. What auralization is, and why it matters

Auralization is an abstract idea, and every time I explain it to someone, it takes a while. Comparing it with visualization may make the job easier.

When we watch one of China’s outlandish TV dramas about the war against Japan, we see scenes from decades ago: scenes we never lived through are brought back for our eyes to see. In a cinema, with 3D glasses on, the visuals feel even more real.

But if the sound isn’t reproduced convincingly, it won’t feel real, however good the visuals are. Say a bomb explodes in front of you, but you hear it behind you. When sight and hearing don’t match, people react like this ↓

Kleiner’s definition of auralization from 1993 [1]:

“By analogy with visualization, auralization is the process of making a known or unknown environment acoustically known.”

Auralization is the term used to describe the process of making a known or unknown environment acoustically known in analogy with visualization.

Professor Vorländer’s definition from 2007 [2]:

“Auralization is the technique of creating audible sound files from simulated, measured or synthesized data.”

My own summary: auralization is the process of moving the acoustic environment of the real world into a virtual one.

That is why auralization is so closely tied to virtual reality. Whether on a computer, through VR or AR glasses, or in an immersive virtual environment, recreating an acoustic environment through auralization always has something “virtual” about it.

So the question is: what is it good for?

Again it was Kleiner, in his 1993 review “Auralization: An overview,” who laid out, with great foresight, the many uses of auralization. Under some of the points I have added my own understanding and explanations; for the others I’m not quite sure what the author had in mind. After all, I don’t know much about the ’90s -_-

  • Training architects, acousticians and audio experts

In the early design stage of a concert hall, for example, once the architectural 3D model exists, auralization lets acousticians assess the acoustic environment, so that room acoustics is taken into account from the very start. See my article on architectural acoustics:

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

  • Training musicians

A start-up founded by a few senior colleagues from the institute where I did my PhD makes 3D in-ear monitoring: on stage or off, musicians can freely move each instrument around in their mix, upgrading from stereo to 3D sound.

3D in-ear monitor mixing [klang.com/en/home]

  • Training blind people

Blind people can echolocate: by clicking their tongues, they can sense the space around them, though not as precisely as bats. Auralization in a virtual environment can simulate all kinds of real acoustic environments and so train echolocation more efficiently. Professor Maarten Hornikx at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands is researching this[3].

A blind man rides a bike using echolocation [YouTube channel: Inside Edition]

  • Predicting factory noise

  • Assessing noise quality

  • Psychoacoustic research

This is an enormous area. Binaural technology, for instance, can recreate the acoustics of a classroom in a virtual environment to study how room acoustics affects children with hearing impairments.
Or take something I don’t know whether anyone is working on yet: the Acoustic Vehicle Alerting Systems (AVAS) the EU has just made mandatory. Electric vehicles are so quiet at low speed that pedestrians may not notice them at all, so the EU now requires them to play a warning sound through an external loudspeaker when driving slowly. But what sound? Some say noise, some say a symphony, some say human voices. Just imagine how lively a motorway traffic jam or a queue at a red light would be! This is exactly the kind of thing that could go into a virtual environment: use auralization to see how pedestrians react to different AVAS sounds, and settle on the final design from people’s subjective ratings. After all, this rather dubious feature exists to serve people.
Below is Mercedes-Benz’s AVAS design: one moment a jet, the next a sports car. Go figure.

Mercedes-Benz’s AVAS design [mercedes-fans.de/]

In my article on psychoacoustics, I also mentioned that auralization can be used in automotive sound design.
A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

  • Studying rooms and loudspeakers

See the first point above.

  • Studying reverberation enhancement systems

  • Studying microphone pickup patterns and placement

  • Making virtual reality systems more realistic

Auralization and VR go hand in hand here.

  • Game effects

This seems to be where auralization plus VR has been most successful commercially so far… You may have seen VR being promoted in shopping malls. The importance of auralization here goes without saying. Say you’re playing Counter-Strike: an enemy shoots at you from the left, and you spin round to look behind you. You’d be dead in no time. Many games now include binaural HRTF effects, which make for a much better experience.

  • Binaural sound for in-flight entertainment

  • Better stereo reproduction in cars

  • Conveying non-acoustic data, for example passing radar signals to pilots as sound when their visual channel is saturated

When I visited Arup in the Netherlands, they told me about an industrial example.

Residents living near a stretch of railway complained that passing trains were too loud and asked the government to do something about it. The government turned to Arup. Arup simulated the pass-by noise with and without various noise barriers and, through auralization, had 25,000 residents and decision-makers listen to the results, so that they could decide together which barrier design to adopt (see the first video at the link below). Try talking decibels with residents and decision-makers, and see how far that gets you!

https://www.arup.com/perspectives/soundlab

2. A not-so-long history

1913

In his JASA article “What exactly is meant by the term ‘auralization’?” [4], Jason E. Summers notes that the term was first used in 1913 by T. Matthay [5]:

ability keenly to visualize, or auralize things apart from their actual physical happening.

He described auralization as the “power of pre-hearing.”

1929

According to Professor Vorländer’s book, Spandöck and his colleagues in Munich tried to reproduce, in a model room on a tabletop, sound signals measured in a real room. The concept took shape quickly, but reality was harsh, and it proved extremely hard to put into practice [6].

1949

Magnetic tape had arrived. Spandöck and his colleagues finally realized their dream, achieving auralization in a scale-model room using ultrasonic signals, the model and a tape recorder. Their technique already contained the seeds of modern auralization: sound field modeling, arbitrary source signals and sound reproduction.

The 1960s

With the development of computers came acoustic simulation, and Schroeder redefined auralization. In 1968, Krokstad introduced the first room acoustics simulation software.

1990

Processor speed, memory and convolution hardware had advanced far enough that room acoustics could be simulated on a personal computer.

1993

Kleiner redefined auralization once more, and his definition is still in use today. His review became a classic in the history of the field.

2007

If Kleiner’s review is a classic, Professor Vorländer’s Auralization is the field’s magnum opus. He also made a successful move from room acoustics to virtual acoustics, and he is something like the founding father of this school.

The best-known universities and professors working on auralization and virtual acoustics today include:

RWTH Aachen University, Germany: Michael Vorländer

Aalto University, Finland: Tapio Lokki. Here are three important papers from his lab:

  • Savioja, L., Huopaniemi, J., Lokki, T., & Väänänen, R. (1999). Creating interactive virtual acoustic environments. Journal of the Audio Engineering Society, 47(9), 675–705.

  • Savioja, L. (1999). Modeling techniques for virtual acoustics. Simulation, 45(10), 10.

  • Lokki, T. (2002). Physically-based auralization: design, implementation, and evaluation. Helsinki University of Technology.

Sorbonne University, France: Brian Katz

Empa, Switzerland: Reto Pieren

In industry, the leader is undoubtedly Facebook Reality Labs, formerly Oculus, which is investing heavily in this area. They approached me last year, but before we got into any real discussion, the whole thing fizzled out because my preferred start date clashed with the visa timeline. Very few other companies work on auralization. Arup, mentioned above, and NLR in the Netherlands do some. Some departments at the major German carmakers and large suppliers, such as Bosch, also have VR labs that do some auralization and automotive acoustics, though on a small scale. In the US, NASA has been at it for a long time. In China, I hear that Shidai Tuoling is working on it.

As I said earlier, in industry auralization seems to have found a home only in gaming. After the VR boom faded, academic research carried on and is still making steady progress. Finding the right point of entry into industry is therefore the key to commercializing auralization.

3. The technology of auralization

Auralization needs three elements:

a source, propagation and reproduction.

As shown in the figure below.

In a nutshell, the process is to convolve the source signal with the response of the propagation environment and play the result to the listener through a suitable reproduction method.

Below I give a brief introduction to each element, so you get a rough idea. I will cover each one in detail in three separate articles later.

The source

In my view, the source is the least studied of the three elements. Yet as the first link in the auralization chain, it is crucial: if the source model is wrong, no amount of accuracy in the propagation model or precision in the reproduction can save it.

Let me borrow a slide from a lecture I gave at TU/e to look at how sources are classified.

Sounds people want to hear, or can accept, include music, speech, birdsong, running water and so on; anything unwanted is lumped together as noise. Of course, this varies from person to person. Some people love rock music; others think it is nothing but howling and wailing.

In terms of how hard they are to model for auralization, sources can be classified by extent, into point, line and area sources, or by motion, into stationary and moving sources. Of these, point sources and stationary sources are the easier ones to model.

Source modeling has three key ingredients: the signal, the position in space and the directivity. The position is easy to obtain; the signal and the directivity are the hard parts.

There are roughly three ways to obtain a source model (signal):

  1. Direct recording. To get a “clean” source sound, it is best to record the dry sound in an anechoic chamber. The trouble is that many sources cannot be recorded in an anechoic chamber, such as the aerodynamic noise of cars, or the noise of large vehicles like planes and trains as they move.

  2. Forward models. The source is synthesized directly from physical models or empirical formulas, though some parameters may have to be measured. Notable successes here include the work of Dr. Reto Pieren at Empa, mentioned above, and Stephen A. Rizzi at NASA. I have met them at conferences and have taken part in several of the VASTCON auralization events they organized.

  3. Inverse models. Put simply, when no forward model is available, the source signal has to be recovered from measured data, that is, from recordings. This was the main subject of my PhD. I described some of my PhD research in a Zhihu answer:

    https://www.zhihu.com/question/309785896/answer/587792267

Directivity is usually measured in an anechoic chamber. For sources that are hard to measure in the lab, such as engine or tire noise, there are empirical formulas that give a rough estimate.

Propagation models

For the first few decades of auralization, geometric acoustics models dominated. Over the past twenty years, as computing power has grown rapidly, numerical acoustics models have come into their own. For interactive auralization, however, numerical models cannot yet run in real time.

Numerical acoustics models: BEM, FEM, FDTD, DG and others;

Geometric acoustics models: image sources, ray tracing.

Geometric models ignore the wave nature of sound and treat it as rays. Important propagation phenomena such as diffraction and scattering are left out. This simplifies sound propagation, so the computation is fast, but the accuracy is poor.

Numerical models are far more accurate and can compute sound propagation in complex environments. The price is obvious: they are much slower and cannot yet run in real time. But as computers get faster, there is plenty to look forward to.

Signal processing and reproduction

Before playback, signal processing is clearly the key. It means convolving the source signal with the response, tracking the positions of the listener and the source, adding the directivity of the source and of the listener, that is, the HRTF (head-related transfer function), and then “delivering it loud and clear to every ear.” For interactive real-time auralization, the latency must stay below the threshold at which people can hear the difference: 20 ms. Real-time auralization therefore makes heavy demands on signal-processing speed.

What does real-time auralization mean? The listener can move around freely during auralization, and the sound field updates in real time. A tracker follows the position and orientation of the listener’s head. The main things to update are the level, which falls off with distance as 1/r and so depends on position, and, depending on the orientation of the head, the source directivity and the HRTF.

There are two main ways to reproduce the sound: headphones and loudspeakers.

Headphones are relatively simple. Given the listener’s HRTF, the signal obtained by convolving the source with the response is convolved again with the HRTF. But HRTFs that are not individualized cause plenty of problems, such as in-head localization and front-back confusion.

Loudspeakers are a more natural way to reproduce sound. But you can’t have an anechoic chamber everywhere, so the influence of the playback room is the main problem. Common methods today include Ambisonics, CTC and VBAP.

Afterword

The more familiar the subject, the harder it is to write about. After writing histories of architectural acoustics, psychoacoustics and sound visualization, I finally made up my mind to tackle auralization. Although I stopped working on auralization after my PhD, I have always found the field fascinating. I hope this article, and the three that will follow, help more people in China get to know auralization, and that others will come along to take the field further.
